title: He Went Wicketless in His First Test. On Sunday in Mullanpur, Saleem Took Six.
excerpt: The 23-year-old Afghan fast bowler terrorised India's batting line-up with pace and reverse swing, but it was not enough to prevent the hosts from declaring at 564 for 8.
body:
Mohammad Saleem had nothing to show for his first Test match. Picked for Afghanistan's one-off game against Zimbabwe earlier this year, the young fast bowler could not find a single wicket. It was the kind of forgettable debut that might have ended a career before it started.

On Sunday in Mullanpur, Saleem ensured nobody would forget him again. Bowling at speeds consistently above 140 kilometres per hour, the 23-year-old ripped through India's batting order to claim his maiden six-wicket haul, finishing with figures that will be the pride of Afghan cricket for years to come.

## The Carnage Began on Saturday

Saleem had already shown his class on Day 1, picking up two wickets in the evening session as India piled up 368 for 3 at stumps. KL Rahul, who had survived a reprieve when Afghanistan inexplicably failed to review a clear edge, went on to complete his 12th Test century. Sai Sudharsan contributed 81 before Saleem found his outside edge and sent him back.

But Saturday was just the appetiser. The real damage came on Sunday morning.

## Breaking the Gill-Pant Stand

Shubman Gill and Rishabh Pant had resumed on overnight scores of 103 and 50, locked in a partnership that had already crossed 100 runs. Together, they extended it to 169 before Saleem struck.

The delivery to Gill was a masterclass. Pitching on a good length and holding its line outside off stump, it drew the Indian captain into a drive. The nick carried cleanly to wicketkeeper Afsar Zazai. Gill departed for 126, his 11th Test century and the second-fastest thousand Test runs by an Indian captain, trailing only Sunil Gavaskar.

Afghanistan should have had him earlier. When Gill was on 108, Azmatullah Omarzai struck him on the pads. The umpire gave it not out, and Afghanistan chose not to review. Ball-tracking showed the delivery was hitting leg stump.

Saleem was not done. Within a few overs, he got the ball to nip back sharply and crash into the top of Dhruv Jurel's off stump. Jurel, who had shouldered arms expecting the ball to pass outside off, was beaten comprehensively. He walked back for 19 off 20 balls.

## Pant Falls, But India Keep Scoring

Pant, who had added 31 to his overnight score, was eyeing a second Test century under the captaincy of Gill. It was not a bowler who ended his innings but Afghanistan captain Hashmatullah Shahidi, who tossed up a flighted delivery that deceived the left-hander. Pant swung hard, mistimed the shot, and Omarzai completed the catch at long-off. He fell for 81.

India were 460 for 6, but the lower order was far from finished. Debutant Manav Suthar and Washington Sundar put on 50 for the seventh wicket, both batting with the confidence of batters who knew time was on their side. Suthar hit Shahidi for a six that took India past 500.

## Saleem's Five and Six

After lunch, Saleem found Suthar's edge with an angled delivery, the ball taking a faint nick on its way through to the keeper. The 23-year-old sank to the ground, touching his forehead to the turf in celebration. Five wickets. His maiden five-wicket haul in Test cricket.

Mohammed Siraj then walked in and treated the Afghan bowlers with disdain. He smashed 14 runs off a single over from debutant left-arm spinner Nangeyalia Kharote — a six followed by two fours — racing to 22 off just 12 balls. It was the most aggressive cameo of the match.

Saleem ended it with the delivery of the day. A full-length ball that reversed through Siraj's defences and uprooted his middle stump. Six for Saleem. India were all out — or rather, declared — at 564 for 8, with Washington Sundar unbeaten on a composed 52.

## Suthar Strikes Immediately

The evening session belonged to India. Manav Suthar, the 22-year-old debutant from Sri Ganganagar near the Pakistan border, was handed the ball in the sixth over of Afghanistan's reply. His first delivery in international cricket turned sharply, and by the end of the over, Abdul Malik had edged to Siraj for 16. Afghanistan were 28 for 1 at tea.

After the break, Prasidh Krishna produced a delivery that split the gap between Sediqullah Atal's bat and pad, crashing into the stumps. Atal departed for 17.

Then Suthar struck again, getting a ball to grip and turn past Rahmanullah Gurbaz's outside edge. Sai Sudharsan took a sharp catch. Gurbaz gone for 12. Afghanistan were three down with only 62 on the board.

By the 25th over, Rahmat Shah and captain Shahidi were fighting to keep the innings alive at 77 for 3, still trailing by 487 runs. The match, barring rain, is heading for an early finish.

## What It Means

For Saleem, this was the announcement of a career. Going from zero wickets in his Test debut to six in his second match represents the kind of leap that separates the talented from the truly determined. His pace, his ability to move the ball both ways, and his skill with the reverse-swinging ball mark him as Afghanistan's most exciting bowling prospect since Rashid Khan first baffled batters in white-ball cricket.

For India, the declaration was a statement of dominance. Five batters scored fifty or more, a depth of batting that few teams in the world can match. And the early wickets in Afghanistan's reply suggest the match will not extend beyond Day 3.

But the lasting image of Day 2 in Mullanpur may be of a young Afghan fast bowler, on his knees after his fifth wicket, forehead pressed to the ground, in a Test he is almost certainly going to lose. That is what Test cricket does at its best — it lets you lose the match but win the moment.

*Sources: Reuters, Bhaskar English, Dubai Telegraph*
